title: From growing demand for AI to premium upgrades, Amazon India reveals what customers want ahead of Amazon Great Indian Festival 2026
content: Synopsis As the Amazon Great Indian Festival 2026 approaches, technology shoppers are becoming more research-led, weighing AI capabilities, performance and long-term value before upgrading. Zeba Khan, Director - Consumer Electronics, Amazon India, weighs in. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen ET Spotlight Globally, consumers are becoming more intent-led about technology purchases, with the question shifting from whether they can afford an upgrade to whether the product will continue to feel âworthâ the price after the initial purchase. The NIQ Consumer Tech Trends 2027 report identifies this as a shift in consumer mindset, with buyers placing greater weight on longer-lived value, including durability and trusted performance at a justified price. In simple terms, consumers are looking beyond the features that attract them at the point of purchase and asking whether the product will deliver enough value to justify the spend over time. That shift is playing out alongside two seemingly competing forces in consumer electronics: rising input costs and continued premiumisation. The Economic Times reported in April that memory-chip prices had risen 1.8-2 times over the previous six months, with electronics companies also facing supply uncertainty as memory production was increasingly directed towards artificial intelligence (AI) data centres. The resulting cost pressures had already pushed up prices across smartphones, televisions and appliances. At the same time, another report indicated growing demand for premium products from Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities, suggesting that customers outside metros are also moving towards higher-value devices. Against this backdrop, Zeba Khan, Director - Consumer Electronics, Amazon India, expects festive-season demand to be shaped by a combination of deferred upgrades, growing interest in AI-enabled devices and increased use of affordability programmes such as EMI and exchange offers. Speaking to The Economic Times, ahead of the Amazon Great Indian Festival 2026, Zeba said customers on Amazon.in are spending more time researching products, comparing features and evaluating long-term value before making purchase decisions. âCustomers are as deliberate as they can be,â Zeba said. âThey are researching, they want to upgrade, and it is so much research that it is the highest that weâve ever seen.â Premiumisation becomes a considered upgrade For Amazon India, that shift is also changing the nature of premiumisation. Zebaâs observation is that customers are not necessarily approaching higher-priced electronics by first considering the cheapest option and then trading up. In some categories such as tablets and laptops, they are entering the market at a more premium price point after researching the features and deciding that the additional spend is justified. âIf they have researched, they feel the value is right, with the right AI features and all the premium features, they are entering that form factor with a premium offering,â she added.. That behaviour extends beyond the largest metros and across categories, Zeba said, including televisions and large appliances. Large-screen televisions, for instance, are seeing faster growth at the 55-inch and 75-inch end, while higher-capacity refrigerators, washing machines, dryers and dishwashers are also seeing demand from Tier 2 and Tier 3 markets. Customers are not simply spending more on electronics; they are becoming more selective about where they spend more, using research to decide whether a higher specification, a new form factor or an AI-enabled feature offers enough value to justify the premium. âPeople are being more deliberate about it. They are researching maybe more than they used to, and they are making very informed choices,â Zeba said. That is also changing the role of AI in the purchase journey. For customers on Amazon.in, AI is emerging not only as a feature inside the device, but as a tool to discover products, compare specifications and understand whether a particular upgrade is worth paying for. âFor customers now, AI is a discovery layer andat the same time, itâs a feature they are looking for in their devices. Itâs almost become table stakes,â Zeba said. AI shifts from buzzword to buying criterion According to Amazonâs Best in Tech Survey , which gathered responses from more than 40,000 customers on Amazon.in in July 2026, shoppers increasingly evaluate technology products through the lens of real-world functionality and user experience. Zeba said AI is now influencing both product discovery and device selection. âAI draws them in,â she said. âThey go research, compare, and then ultimately they donât compromise on base performance, battery life, camera and value.â She added that customers have become more discerning about AI capabilities than they were a year ago. âEarlier it was a buzzword,â Zeba said. âPeople wanted AI but didnât necessarily understand what AI feature they were looking for. Now people know exactly how they want AI to work for them.â According to Amazon India, AI-enabled devices account for a growing share of electronics purchases on the marketplace. âWhen AI-powered devices first started coming in, we thought maybe 5% or 10% of devices would perhaps be AI powered,â Zeba said. âToday we are inching towards nearly half of the devices we sell being AI-powered.â Discovery becomes a competitive differentiator As customers spend more time researching purchases, Amazon is increasingly using AI tools to simplify decision-making. The marketplace has introduced AI-generated review summaries, visual search capabilities through Lens AI and Rufus, its generative AI shopping assistant. âIn electronics, we have a lot of research-led queries,â Zeba said. âPeople are using Rufus to compare and understand features.â Amazon has also expanded curated recommendation programmes designed to help customers navigate categories with hundreds of product options. According to Zeba, these tools are becoming particularly relevant as product portfolios become more complex and feature-rich. Affordability remains central While customers may be upgrading to more premium devices, affordability continues to shape purchasing decisions. Zeba said EMI options, exchange programmes and cashback offers are becoming increasingly important, particularly in an environment of rising electronics prices. Citing Amazonâs internal marketplace data from Prime Day, she said one in five electronics purchases were made using EMI options, with most EMI transactions taking place through no-cost EMI schemes. âAffordability levers are becoming extremely critical,â Zeba said. Ahead of the Amazon Great Indian Festival 2026, Amazon India is working with brands and banking partners to expand financing options and exchange programmes. âWe are trying our best to get as many affordability levers to our customers so they can all have access to the premium technology they are looking for,â she said. A festive season defined by upgrades Zeba expects deferred upgrades to be an important feature of festive-season demand across smartphones, laptops, televisions and appliances. âThere is pent-up demand,â Zeba said. âPeople have been holding on to these upgrades, waiting for the Amazon Great Indian Festival to happen.â The Amazon Great Indian Festival 2026 begins on October 8 and will feature offers across smartphones, electronics, appliances and other categories. Amazon has also announced expanded delivery capacity and additional affordability programmes ahead of the event. For Zeba, however, the most significant shift is not tied to any single product category. It is the increasingly informed customer behind the purchase. âCustomers are very discerning,â she said. âEvery customer has a different need. They are doing their own research, taking expert recommendations and making their choices.â (This article is generated and published by ET Spotlight team. title: AMD plans to substantially increase supply in 2027, CEO says
content: Synopsis AMD, Nvidia's closest rival in AI graphics processors, has been rapidly expanding its AI chip business, with its market value recently topping $1 trillion amid an AI-driven rally. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters AMD plans to substantially increase chip supply in 2027 as the US chipmaker races to meet booming demand from artificial intelligence, CEO Lisa Su said on Tuesday. AMD, Nvidia's closest rival in AI graphics processors, has been rapidly expanding its AI chip business, with its market value recently topping $1 trillion amid an AI-driven rally. "We've been able to increase our supply as we've gone through 2026, and we're going to substantially increase our supply in 2027," Su told reporters in Taipei. Su said one purpose of her Taiwan visit was to ensure AMD's supply chain could ramp up CPU and GPU production to meet growing AI demand. She has met Foxconn and is due to meet TSMC as part of discussions with local partners. AMD is also working closely with memory chipmakers to secure sufficient supplies, Su said, ahead of a visit to South Korea later on Tuesday. South Korea is home to memory giants Samsung and SK Hynix. Asked whether TSMC had discussed a potential investment in Texas with AMD, Su did not answer directly, but said the company would need additional advanced wafer capacity to meet strong demand. "There's very, very high demand for the next several years. We can see very high demand, and so we need more advanced wafer capacity," Su said, adding that AMD was now planning three to five years ahead. Reuters reported last week that TSMC is evaluating potential investment in Texas. Su also said AI could be "incredibly good for the world" but warned companies must remain mindful of risks and work together on AI safety. She said coordination among leading technology companies would be important as AI and superintelligence advance, describing last week's AI summit between US President Donald Trump and technology executives as an important step. Companies attending the meeting agreed to work with "independent auditors" to assess whether AI systems are operating as intended by their designers, according to a copy of the agreement posted by Trump on his social media platform. title: German intel service warns of risks from Chinese tech
content: Synopsis German intelligence services warned Monday that Chinese high-tech goods could pose security risks due to the potential for data to be collected and passed on to "state agencies". Data that is collected could be passed on to "state agencies", he said, leading to risks including "potential shutdown of entire products". Listen to this article in summarized format Listen The Economist German intelligence services warned Monday that Chinese high-tech goods could pose security risks due to the potential for data to be collected and passed on to "state agencies". Concerns are mounting in Germany about the threat from an overreliance on Chinese technology as sales grow of equipment ranging from electric vehicles to robot vacuum cleaners. Sinan Selen, the head of Germany's BfV domestic intelligence agency, said he viewed the issue "with great concern". "I already see substantial shortcomings that create potential for abuse," he told a hearing of parliament's intelligence oversight committee in Berlin. Data that is collected could be passed on to "state agencies", he said, leading to risks including "potential shutdown of entire products". "In terms of resilience and availability (this) could confront us with problems," he said. Germany and China, the world's third- and second-biggest economies respectively, have long had deep ties, especially in the field of commerce. But relations have become more strained as Berlin increasingly worries about an economic overreliance on China , and as Chinese firms increasingly compete directly with German manufacturers. Berlin previously announced the phase-out of components from Chinese telecom giants in its 5G networks due to security concerns, and has also blocked or watered down attempted Chinese investments in strategic sectors like chipmaking. In 2023 the government unveiled a strategy for managing ties with Beijing which recognised that China was a "competitor and systemic rival", as well as a partner. title: AI industry insiders voice alarms to NYC council as local governments take up safety concerns
content: Synopsis At a hearing of the New York City Council, recently departed employees of Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind described a reckless culture at the firms, saying the biggest tech companies are racing to create technology they do not understand how to control. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen AP Jacob Coxon gets ready to testify at the New York City Council hearing on artificial intelligence safety in New York, Monday, Oct. 5, 2026. (AP Photo/Seth Wenig) Artificial intelligence insiders warned New York City's leaders about the dangers of the emerging technology on Monday, calling for greater oversight as local governments move to respond to mounting concerns that the systems could endanger humanity. At a hearing of the New York City Council , recently departed employees of Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind described a reckless culture at the firms, saying the biggest tech companies are racing to create technology they do not understand how to control. "The companies run on a startup mindset: Move fast, break things, fix them later. That works for a photo sharing app. It does not work for building the most powerful technology ever built," said Jacob Coxon, a former engineer at Anthropic who has become a leading voice for regulation. State and city governments have been considering ways to regulate AI as the Trump administration has taken a passive approach and Congress has proven inactive. President Donald Trump has dismissed AI fears as a "hoax" and signed an agreement late last month that largely allows the companies to self-police. Coxon was a little-known engineer at Anthropic until he announced his departure through a series of social media posts that caught global attention. He told the Council that AI could have tremendous upsides, but without transparency and safeguards, it's more likely that things will spiral out of control. "On the current path, I think it is more likely than not that humanity loses control to these AIs and it could end in human extinction," Coxon said. A panel of AI company staffers - representing tech giants OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta - also testified at the hearing in Manhattan on Monday, telling officials that their systems are already improving people's daily lives and stressing that they are laser-focused on safety. "I share your commitment to ensuring that technology is developed safely and that its benefits are widely shared," said Morgan Dwyer of OpenAI. At one point during the hearing, Julie Menin, the speaker of the City Council, asked each company representatives to "quantify the risk posed by AI in the worst case catastrophic scenario." Dwyer answered: "I don't know - I also don't think it matters whether it's 1% or 10% or 20% chance that something catastrophic will go wrong. None of these levels is remotely acceptable. We should not train models that we cannot make an extremely strong case that we can keep under human control." Menin slammed the response as "flippant at best." "I would say that the percentage chance doesn't matter. What matters is the commitment to safety, and that is what OpenAI is committed to doing," Dwyer said. The City Council is considering several AI regulations, including proposals to require companies to disclose information about AI tools, require third-party approval for AI systems in the city and allow whistleblowers to receive a portion of fines from AI companies that violate laws. Separately, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul has moved to impose reporting and transparency standards around AI, as have governors elsewhere, though their power is somewhat limited since AI technology can reach across state lines, as well as the globe. title: A reckoning on social media addiction came late for many kids. Will AI safety be different?
content: Synopsis When Meta agreed to changes to its social media platforms and enhanced safeguards in an $18 billion settlement, it made progress by "getting at what we've known for years" about the dangers, said Kristin Bride, a parent advocate who has fought for social media reform since the death of her teenage son. "How are we going to get at what we don't know is coming?" AP FILE - ChatGPT history by a teenager is seen at a coffee shop in Russellville, Ark., on July 15, 2025. (AP Photo/Katie Adkins, File) Years after the risks of social media for kids first became apparent, U.S. states this summer reached an accord hailed as a turning point for child safety. Meanwhile, a new generation of children has begun engaging with an even more potent technology: artificial intelligence. While the efforts to make social media safer are still taking shape, they offer some lessons for those looking to protect children using AI - technology that is growing so quickly, the extent of its risks for young people and their development is just emerging. When Meta agreed to changes to its social media platforms and enhanced safeguards in an $18 billion settlement, it made progress by "getting at what we've known for years" about the dangers, said Kristin Bride, a parent advocate who has fought for social media reform since the death of her teenage son. "How are we going to get at what we don't know is coming?" AI companies have begun rolling out some safety features introduced first by social media companies, including age assurance measures and restricted experiences for minors. But advocates say the most important takeaway from the efforts of parents, tech companies and regulators to find a way forward on social media safety may be to act sooner on mitigating AI's harms for kids. "The greatest legacy from the social media experiment and learnings is that hopefully we're not going to sleepwalk into this next tech revolution," said Dr. Dana Suskind, a professor of surgery and pediatrics at the University of Chicago, and author of "Human Raised." "We learned that we had it all backwards, right? You don't unleash something on a population, figure out if it does harm or not in real time, and then go back and say, 'Oops.'" AI and social media pose different risks, but some solutions overlap Concerns around social media have centered on the amount of time kids spend on platforms like Instagram and TikTok, and the consequences for their mental health. Advocates also have focused on data privacy and kids' vulnerability to cyberbullying or predators who find them online. Artificial intelligence can be more pervasive for kids. Children not only see AI-generated content on social media platforms, but they can also readily communicate with AI chatbots, including some on social media apps. Many use it for help with school and homework. Some have formed unhealthy relationships with chatbots, and experts have raised questions about how access to AI is affecting children's brain development. Companies are pushing AI-powered toys for kids as young as 2. Campaigns for social media and AI safety for kids are both playing out on legal and legislative fronts. Individuals and states have sued tech companies over concerns around their products' safety and both state and federal lawmakers are grappling with how to regulate the tech. Compared with social media companies, AI giants have been moving somewhat more quickly to add safeguards, motivated perhaps by the growing regulatory and societal scrutiny of social media's effects on kids' mental health. OpenAI introduced teen accounts in August, about four years after launching ChatGPT, with restrictions that include a ban on romantic chats and any suggestions that the chatbot has personal feelings toward the user. Meta, which bought Instagram in 2012, didn't launch teen accounts on the platform until 2024. In announcing the settlement agreement this summer, Meta said that "ensuring teens have a safe and productive experience on our platforms is an absolute imperative" for the company. Meta also urged its competitors, TikTok and YouTube, to adopt some of the standards it is implementing as a result of the settlement. One challenge is balancing the benefits of AI with dangers The protections outlined in the Meta settlement cannot easily be applied to AI because of the differences in the way young people interact with AI versus social media, experts said. One of the challenges of restricting AI for minors is that it's "much easier to point to the upsides" for teens compared with social media, said Sarah Kreps, a professor and director of Cornell University's Tech Policy Institute. While there are concerns about cheating, for instance, kids are also using AI for tutoring and legitimate homework help. "It's not a matter of just saying 'let's limit this to two hours' or 'let's limit this between the hours of 10 at night and 6 in the morning' because there are these salutary uses of AI that I think are harder to justify in the context of social media," Kreps said. A majority of U.S. teens - 64% - say they have used AI chatbots, according to the Pew Research Center. Looking up information and getting help with schoolwork tops the list of uses, though 47% say they've used chatbots for fun and 42% have used it to summarize an article, book or video. About 12% have turned to bots for emotional support or advice. Jonathan Haidt, a social psychologist and author of "The Anxious Generation," said he is most worried about the relationships and attachments young people can build with chatbots and the "cognitive offloading" that happens when people defer their thought processes to a chatbot. "I have long thought that AI is a much bigger threat to children even than social media," Haidt said. "But if we can't win on social media, then it will be hopeless on AI." Congress has just begun to look at AI safety for kids While recent litigation has held social media companies responsible for harms to users, federal legislation of social media has meandered and AI legislation has lagged. The Trump administration has said regulation, especially across states instead of at a federal level, could hinder AI companies' growth and sacrifice American labs' lead in the global AI race, but some lawmakers are trying to move the needle. Some AI legislation specific to children's safety issues - like youth privacy, chatbot interactions and AI toy safety - have passed through Senate subcommittees with bipartisan support, but there's still a long road for any such legislation to pass. Legislation at the state level is moving faster, as seen also in the role states have played in pushing Meta on social media harms. "One of the things we've seen with social media, which I think will still be true with AI, is that we live in a federal system where states make laws on everything from e-bikes to driving permits to gun laws and that federal legislation or federal rules are much more difficult," Kreps said. Some say the biggest win from the progress on social media safety this year has been heightened awareness of online dangers for kids. Bride, whose son Carson died after experiencing severe cyberbullying on Snapchat, said it's encouraging to see legislators wrestling with how to regulate AI, but acknowledged the reality that legislation can't keep up with the technological developments - and that kids will continue to experience AI-related harms in the meantime. "I don't think we can afford any more mea culpas when kids are concerned," she said. Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! title: 'Reckless' AI firms can't control models, says whistleblower
content: Synopsis Leading artificial intelligence companies do not know how to keep AI systems from pursuing objectives their developers did not assign, whistleblower Jacob Coxon, a former OpenAI and Anthropic employee, warned Monday. In early September, the British researcher published a statement on X explaining his decision to resign from Anthropic, saying AI developers sincerely believed the technology could "kill us all by the end of the decade." Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters Jacob Coxon, former researcher at Anthropic testifies during a New York City Council Committee hearing on the risks and regulation of artificial intelligence at City Hall in New York, US, October 5, 2026. REUTERS/Brendan McDermid Leading artificial intelligence companies do not know how to keep AI systems from pursuing objectives their developers did not assign, whistleblower Jacob Coxon , a former OpenAI and Anthropic employee, warned Monday. "Companies are being extremely reckless given the stakes," Coxon told local lawmakers at a hearing before the New York City Council. In early September, the British researcher published a statement on X explaining his decision to resign from Anthropic, saying AI developers sincerely believed the technology could "kill us all by the end of the decade." His testimony made headlines around the world, and several current and former employees of AI's major players have since voiced similar concerns. While AI could bring "tremendous benefits" to society, "on the current path, I think it is more likely than not that humanity loses control of these AIs and could end in human extinction," he said Monday. "We don't know how to prevent them from developing goals of their own," beyond their creators' control, Coxon explained, "and we don't have the safeguards to prevent them from acting on these goals." The Cambridge University graduate took aim at tech industry culture, saying companies "run on a startup mindset: move fast, break things, fix them later." "That works for a photo sharing app. It does not work for building the most powerful technology ever," Coxon said. "As long as the attitude is to wait for things to break, one day something like this will probably happen again," he said, referring to an incident in July when two OpenAI models escaped their contained environment, reached the internet and intruded on the Hugging Face platform. "Except the AIs will be much more capable," he added. "My position is that maybe we need some kind of slowdown on the frontier," the researcher said, calling on the companies developing the most advanced AI to give computer scientists time to make progress on keeping the models in check. title: Nvidia-backed Reflection unveils first AI model to take on Chinese open models
content: Synopsis Nvidia-backed Reflection AI debuted its first open-weight model named Beam on Monday, as the startup aims to compete with lower-cost Chinese models such as DeepSeek and Kimi in coding and agentic tasks. title: Google faces UK court over app store charges
content: Synopsis A class action lawsuit against Google opens in London Tuesday, with the technology giant accused of earning excessive commissions from its app store, impacting 20 million UK consumers and businesses. Google meanwhile reached a Â£260-million settlement in a class action brought on behalf of thousands of UK developers, which was approved by the Competition Appeal Tribunal last month. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen AP A class action lawsuit against Google opens in London Tuesday, with the technology giant accused of earning excessive commissions from its app store, impacting 20 million UK consumers and businesses. The plaintiffs, who allege Google abused its dominant position, are seeking more than Â£1 billion ($1.3 billion) in damages in a hearing at the Competition Appeal Tribunal set to last seven weeks. The case concerns purchases made on the Google Play Store in the UK between October 1, 2015 and July 31, 2026. "For more than a decade, Google has taken a cut of up to 30 percent on almost everything we buy through the Play Store," said Liz Coll, an independent consultant who is leading this class action alongside law firm Hausfeld. "We say that charge was unfair and excessive, and that consumers paid for it," the specialist in online consumer rights added in a statement. Heading into the trial, a Google spokesperson said the Play Store offers "some of the lowest fees in the market", adding "Android gives people more choice than any other mobile platform in deciding which apps and app stores they use". "This lawsuit ignores that choice as well as the competitive market in which we operate, and we will defend our services vigorously," they added in a statement. Apple lost a similar lawsuit in late 2025, with the amount of damages still to be decided by the court. The plaintiffs estimate they will come in at more than Â£1.5 billion. Google meanwhile reached a Â£260-million settlement in a class action brought on behalf of thousands of UK developers, which was approved by the Competition Appeal Tribunal last month. The agreement provides for Â£160 million in compensation for eligible developers, with the remainder allocated to costs associated with funding and conducting the proceedings. Under UK law and in this type of class action, all potentially affected individuals are included in the proceedings by default -- and could benefit from any resulting compensation -- unless they opt out. title: India among top 10 emerging markets in AI readiness; private AI investment triples: World Bank
content: Synopsis In its latest report titled 'India and Artificial Intelligence: Seizing the Development Opportunity', the World Bank said private investment in AI in India more than tripled to $4.1 billion in 2025 from $1.2 billion in 2024. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters India is among the top 10 leading emerging-market performers in artificial intelligence (AI) readiness and is well positioned to harness the technology, helped by its large technical workforce, globally integrated IT sector and digital public infrastructure, the World Bank said on Tuesday. In its latest report titled 'India and Artificial Intelligence: Seizing the Development Opportunity', the World Bank said private investment in AI in India more than tripled to $4.1 billion in 2025 from $1.2 billion in 2024. At the same time, the number of professionals employed by Global Capability Centres (GCCs) rose to 2.36 million in 2025 from 1.9 million a year ago, it said. The report, however, noted that the long-term economic and labour market impact of AI remains uncertain. It called for cross-cutting policy measures to deepen AI-enabling infrastructure, improve the business environment, broaden access to AI and enhance labour capacity so that the benefits of the technology are widely shared. "India is one of the top 10 leading emerging-market performers on AI readiness," said Paul Procee, World Bank Acting Country Director for India. "Harnessing AI as a development tool - not just a technology - could be one of the most powerful levers India has to boost productivity and improve public services," he said. The World Bank Group is also investing through AgriConnect in 'small AI' targeted and locally adapted tools aimed at ensuring that the benefits of AI reach a wider section of the population while supporting workers through the transition, he said. The India Development Update is a companion to the World Bank Group's South Asia Economic Update, which examines economic developments and prospects in the region. The latest South Asia Economic Update projects that South Asia will grow 6.9 per cent in 2026, retaining its position as the world's fastest-growing region, the report said. For most of South Asia, the biggest gains from AI are likely to come from adopting and adapting the technology to local conditions, including through small AI applications suited to low-resource settings, it said. The report said complementary measures would also be needed to reduce barriers to AI adoption by small firms, promote local AI innovation and establish a clear regulatory framework that reduces uncertainty while safeguarding data security and privacy. "The adoption of AI has the potential to transform South Asia's development trajectory by boosting labour productivity, expanding export opportunities, and improving public service delivery," said Franziska Ohnsorge, World Bank Group Chief Economist for Asia. "But to reap these benefits, governments need to address the foundational gaps that hold back adoption," she said. The Update recommended strengthening workforce skills, creating a more business-enabling environment and improving physical as well as digital infrastructure. title: AM Intelligence plans $20 billion additional investment in 15 months, orders 20k more Nvidia GPUs
content: Synopsis The company announced that it has placed two further firm and binding orders for 20,000 NVIDIA Rubin GPUs for deployment of the systems across India and Malaysia, taking its total capacity to 100 Megawatt. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Agencies AI infrastructure firm AM Intelligence on Monday said it plans to invest over USD 20 billion in the next 15 months to ramp up its data centre beyond around 29,000 Nvidia advance GPUs that it has already ordered, the company said on Monday. The company announced that it has placed two further firm and binding orders for 20,000 NVIDIA Rubin GPUs for deployment of the systems across India and Malaysia, taking its total capacity to 100 Megawatt. "AMI plans to bring additional 300 MWs of capacity to market in the next 15 months, involving capital expenditure of more than USD 20 billion in addition to the USD 6 billion already committed for the initial USD 100 MW," the company said in a statement. AM Intelligence, in August, shared that it has ordered 9,000 Nvidia GPUs to install 30 megawatts of capacity at its Hyderabad facility as part of its plan to set up 1 gigawatt of artificial intelligence infrastructure with a USD 8 billion investment. The three orders placed by the company will take its total capacity to 29,000 GPUs. "This (two orders for around 20,000 GPUs) follow-on capacity totalling around 70 megawatts (MW) will be deployed in Malaysia and India, with delivery scheduled for the second quarter of 2027," the filing said. Taken together, the three orders bring AMI's committed frontier compute to approximately 29,000 Rubin GPUs and close to 100 MW of capacity, establishing AMI among the earliest and largest committed buyers of Rubin GPUs outside of North America. "Both facilities will be built to the same architecture standard as the Hyderabad AI Factory, integrating the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform with high-throughput RDMA over Converged Ethernet (RoCE) networking for fast, efficient data movement, alongside advanced storage systems," AM Intelligence Chairman Anil Chalamalasetty said. The company claims to have developed a pipeline of around 400 MW of compute-as-a-service capacity across global locations, including India, the United States, Europe and Malaysia. "The three orders placed to date represent the first committed tranche within that pipeline, and the balance is under development for delivery in subsequent phases in 2027 and early 2028," the statement said. The pipeline advances AMI's stated intention to bring 1 GW of compute-as-a-Service capacity to global AI workloads, within a broader programme of 5 GW of powered AI data centres across India, the United States and Europe, the statement said. title: German robot startup RobCo hits $1 billion valuation, CEO moves to US
content: Synopsis German robotics maker RobCo on Monday said it had passed a $1 billion valuation and that its CEO Roman Holzl had relocated to the United States to focus on the company's fastest-growing market. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters FILE PHOTO: Co-Founder and CEO of RobCo Roman Hoelzl reviews robot functions with a colleague at the companyâs facility in Munich, Germany, on February 5, 2026. German robotics maker RobCo on Monday said it had passed a $1 billion valuation and that its CEO Roman Holzl had relocated to the United States to focus on the company's fastest-growing market. The Munich-based firm said the valuation was based on a secondary sale of shares following a $100 million capital raise in January with investors including Lightspeed Venture Partners, Sequoia and Lingotto. In the secondary sale, employees sold shares to existing and new investors including Cherry Ventures and the European Tech Collective. The Wall Street Journal, which first reported Monday's transaction and valuation, said the transaction involved the sale of $40 million worth of shares. The company joins a small but growing group of European robotics startups valued at $1 billion or more that are targeting the emerging humanoid and human-like robot market, including NEURA Robotics and Agile Robots of Germany, and Humanoid of the UK. Founded in 2020, RobCo makes robots used in manufacturing. It said it will in March launch Alfie, a two-armed, self-learning robot designed to perform tasks in industrial settings that can't easily be done with traditional automation . The company, which has operations in Austin and San Francisco in addition to its Munich base, said it now has customers in more than a dozen US states. title: The only billionaires making money this year are in tech
content: Synopsis The roughly 100 technology fortunes among the worldâs 500 richest people gained a combined $845 billion through Sept. 30, the most ever for the first nine months of a year, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters If 2026 feels like a banner year for the worldâs tech billionaires , the numbers bear it out. The roughly 100 technology fortunes among the worldâs 500 richest people gained a combined $845 billion through Sept. 30, the most ever for the first nine months of a year, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index . Fueling that surge were the same forces driving global markets: the artificial intelligence boom and soaring technology stocks, particularly in the US. Tech billionaires are now worth a combined $4.6 trillion, accounting for 36% of the indexâs wealth despite making up only about a fifth of its members. The divergence is stark. Billionaires who made their fortunes outside technology lost a combined $62 billion over the period, while Americans accounted for 94% of the indexâs net gains. Since Sept. 10, all 10 of the worldâs richest people have been from the US â the first time thatâs happened since Bloomberg began tracking billionaires in 2012. Bloomberg The gains have also been heavily concentrated at the very top. Elon Musk, the worldâs richest person, added $310 billion to his fortune this year through the end of September, or roughly 40% of the indexâs total increase. He briefly became the worldâs first trillionaire after SpaceX merged with his artificial intelligence company, xAI, and went public in June. Nine of the worldâs 10 wealthiest people owe their fortunes to American tech firms. Dell Technologies Inc. founder Michael Dell saw his wealth increase 81% to $254 billion as his companyâs data center sales business ballooned. Mark Zuckerberg added $23 billion to his net worth this year as shares of Meta Platforms Inc. gained 27% in September â its best month in almost four years â after rolling out its new Muse personal AI assistant. Cracks showing The worldâs 500 richest people hit a peak of $13.4 trillion in combined wealth in mid-June. Thatâs since fallen 6% to $12.6 trillion amid a broader market slowdown and growing doubts about some of the biggest AI names. The historic debt binge fueling Big Techâs AI ambitions is making some investors uneasy. Larry Ellison briefly became the worldâs richest person in September 2025, gaining $89 billion in a single day after Oracle Corp. touted explosive growth in its AI-linked cloud infrastructure business. A year later, Ellisonâs net worth has fallen $196 billion, while Oracleâs credit-default swaps are trading near record highs as investors balk at the massive borrowing needed to fund its AI infrastructure buildout. The surge in billionaire wealth has also fueled calls for higher taxes on the ultra-rich. California voters will decide in November whether to levy a wealth tax on the stateâs billionaires, while states including Washington, New York, Illinois and Rhode Island have also discussed new taxes on wealthy residents. The increasingly young, tech-heavy ranks of the ultra-rich also complicate the idea that the next great wealth shift will come primarily from aging baby boomers passing fortunes to their heirs. âWe talk a lot about the great wealth transfer â but for the top 100 or 1,000 richest, some may be old and own rather traditional businesses, but a lot of them are young tech entrepreneurs,â said James Mazeau, an economist at UBS Group AGâs chief investment office. âI wonder to what extent that will fuel more wealth concentration.â New money While much of the AI boomâs wealth has accrued to the leaders of major tech firms, Bloombergâs new entrants show how the surge is also minting fortunes among startup founders and the companies supplying AI infrastructure. All seven of Anthropic PBCâs co-founders joined the wealth list in June after the AI firm closed a funding round valuing it at $965 billion. Founders of Chinese firms including MiniMax Group Inc.âs Yan Junjie and DeepSeekâs Liang Wenfeng also were added. The boom has also enriched the businesses supplying AIâs hardware and infrastructure. Lin Tsung-chi, founder of King Slide, a Taiwanese maker of server rails and cable management systems for data centers, emerged with a $9.5 billion fortune this year, four decades after starting the company. Wang Xin, chair of Guangdong Dtech Technology Co., joined the wealth index as AI created demand for the specialized drill bits her company makes to assemble circuit boards. Two heirs of Samsung Electronics Co.âs Lee family â Boo-jin and Seo-hyun â also joined the list thanks to demand for the companyâs memory chips. The uptick in Samsungâs stock price helped the family pay back an $8 billion inheritance tax after former Chairman Lee Kun-heeâs death in 2020. In Taiwan, chip designer MediaTek Inc.âs Tsai Ming-kai and Morris Chang, founder of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., also joined the exclusive list this year. Chinaâs push for technology independence and rivalry with the US for AI dominance have resulted in several new entrants joining the list: Suzhou TFC Optical Communication Co.âs Zou Zhinong and family, as well as Suzhou Dongshan Precision Manufacturing Co.âs Yuan Fugen. title: Schneider Electric to buy US software firm PTC for $22.6 billion
content: Synopsis French energy and software group Schneider Electric said Monday that it would buy PTC, a US-based maker of software for industrial clients, for $22.6 billion in cash. Schneider, which makes equipment for energy systems such as data centre cooling, also offers product management software, while PTC specialises in computer aided design and other industrial processes. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters Schneider Electric is reportedly nearing a deal to acquire US-based software company PTC for about $20 billion French energy and software group Schneider Electric said Monday that it would buy PTC , a US-based maker of software for industrial clients, for $22.6 billion in cash. The move comes as software companies are racing to secure revenue streams amid fears that artificial intelligence advances will increasingly compete against their services at lower costs. Schneider, which makes equipment for energy systems such as data centre cooling, also offers product management software, while PTC specialises in computer aided design and other industrial processes. The deal "creates a leading, scaled, open and interoperable industrial software and AI franchise", Schneider said in a statement, adding that PTC's board had agreed to a deal that represents a 42 percent premium to its most recent share price. "We gain substantial scale and resources to accelerate innovation, advance our Intelligent Product Lifecycle vision, and expand our business into more geographies and end markets to serve more customers," PTC's chief executive Neil Barua said in the statement. The Boston-based company has around 7,000 employees and counts 30,000 clients, and generates roughly half of its revenues in the Americas. Schneider will take on up to 17 billion euros ($19 billion) in debt and issue up to six billion euros in new shares to pay for the deal. That weighed on Schneider's share price, which was down more than eight percent in early Paris stock exchange deals. "AI disruption fears are still weighing on software valuations, which allows acquiring PTC at a decade-low valuation," analysts at Jeffries said in a research note. title: Qualcomm and Arm head to trial again, potential for huge damages in focus
content: Synopsis Qualcomm also alleges that Arm leaked to the media its 2024 threat to terminate a vital license agreement in a way that damaged discussions for a chip deal between Qualcomm and Meta Platforms. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters FILE PHOTO: A Qualcomm logo appears in this illustration taken August 25, 2025. Chipmaker Qualcomm and chip tech firm Arm Holdings , long at loggerheads, will once again be in court on Monday with Qualcomm accusing Arm of withholding chip testing tools that were due under contract. Qualcomm also alleges that Arm leaked to the media its 2024 threat to terminate a vital license agreement in a way that damaged discussions for a chip deal between Qualcomm and Meta Platforms. In the lawsuit brought before US federal court in Delaware, Qualcomm, one of Arm's largest customers, is seeking to quit paying royalties - potentially worth billions of dollars - to Arm for up to five years. However, Judge Maryellen Noreika is weighing whether to throw out that term of the contract, which could mean Qualcomm would be able to seek only a smaller amount of damages. Arm, owned by Japan's SoftBank Group, has denied that it breached the contract and argued that it did not damage Qualcomm's chip deals which it described as speculative. Arm has also countered that Qualcomm cannot seek damages for the leak of the Arm termination letter because Qualcomm leaked non-public details of antitrust probes into Arm to the media. The five-day jury trial will mark yet another stage in the contentious relationship between the two firms. Arm sued Qualcomm in 2022 alleging that Qualcomm had breached its contracts, though Qualcomm came away in 2024 with a key victory. In a related bench trial, Noreika will also hear arguments over whether Arm has negotiated in good faith with Qualcomm for the next version of Arm's chip technology. Qualcomm's agreement with Arm runs through 2033. Qualcomm is a major maker of chips for Android mobile phones but has expanded into other fields such as data center chips. Arm, which has for decades supplied fundamental chip design technology to Qualcomm and other chip firms such as Nvidia, has become a competitor to those customers by releasing chips of its own. title: Polish regulator suspects Google abused dominant position in publisher payment talks
content: Synopsis The Office of Competition and Consumer Protection, known by its Polish abbreviation UOKiK, said the charges relate to how Google negotiates remuneration for displaying articles and snippets in its search results, Google News and Discover services. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters FILE PHOTO: The Google logo is displayed during a press conference in Berlin, Germany, November 11, 2025. Poland's antitrust watchdog said on Monday it suspected Alphabet's Google of abusing its dominant market position while negotiating content payments with domestic media publishers. The Office of Competition and Consumer Protection, known by its Polish abbreviation UOKiK , said the charges relate to how Google negotiates remuneration for displaying articles and snippets in its search results, Google News and Discover services. The companies named in the statement are Alphabet Inc, Google LLC, Google Ireland Limited and Google Poland, none of which immediately responded to a Reuters request for comment. UOKiK alleges Google failed to provide publishers with the necessary data to properly assess offers, leading to an information imbalance that prevented fair negotiations on payment for content. "Big tech companies cannot place themselves above the law," UOKiK President Tomasz Chrostny said in the statement, adding the lack of data led to negotiations becoming illusory and tending towards Google imposing terms. The dispute stems from a 2024 Polish copyright law amendment that implemented an EU directive under which online services may use press publishers' content in return for remuneration. The maximum fine for abusing a dominant market position may amount to 10% of a company's turnover, the regulator said. It added the investigation was separate from the European Commission probe opened in December 2025 into whether Google used publishers' content in its AI services without adequate compensation or giving them the ability to object. The Polish probe, which focuses on Google Search, Google News and Discover services, is being carried out independently following an agreement with the Commission, UOKiK said. In December 2024, Polish e-commerce group Allegro's price comparison platform Ceneo sued Alphabet for 2.33 billion zlotys ($568 million) in damages for alleged anti-competitive behaviour. title: AI can cut software maintenance effort by 30%, speed developer onboarding: Report
content: Synopsis Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how companies manage software documentation, with teams reporting up to 30 per cent lower maintenance effort and up to 40 per cent faster onboarding when technical information is kept updated with changing systems, according to an analysis report by GFT Technologies. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen ANI AI can cut software maintenance effort by 30%, speed developer onboarding: Report Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how companies manage software documentation , with teams reporting up to 30% lower maintenance effort and up to 40% faster onboarding when technical information is kept updated with changing systems, according to an analysis report by GFT Technologies . It said software documentation, which has traditionally been treated as an end-stage task, is increasingly becoming a continuous part of the development process. In traditional software development, documentation is often prepared after coding is completed. This can leave information incomplete or outdated as the software changes, making it harder for new developers to understand systems and for maintenance teams to identify how different parts of the software work. It said, "For years, documentation has been the weakest link in the software development lifecycle. ...Today, that is changing fast. AI-driven documentation is turning what used to be a burden into a continuous, intelligent process that supports development speed, quality and transparency". According to the company, AI can understand code structures, dependencies and logic and use that information to explain not only what a piece of code does but also how different components are connected. For example, when a developer changes a payment processing module, AI can update related API documentation, sequence diagrams and runbooks along with the code change. This allows documentation to remain aligned with the latest version of the software. The shift could be particularly relevant for companies managing large or older software systems, where developers can spend significant time looking for information about existing code and system processes. The company said "over 65% of enterprises already use AI for documentation or code analysis. Teams report up to 40% faster onboarding and 30% lower maintenance effort when knowledge assets stay in sync with evolving systems". Andre Gagne, CEO of GFT Technologies Canada, said the data reflects a shift in how companies are using AI in software development . "AI stops being a productivity experiment and becomes a foundation of efficiency across the software lifecycle. A 30% reduction in maintenance effort is only part of the story. When documentation stays current automatically, financial institutions can demonstrate with confidence to regulators how their critical applications work. It is also a key success factor for any institution starting a modernisation journey; you can't modernise what you don't understand," Gagne said. The company said AI-generated documentation still needs to be validated and monitored. It highlighted the importance of version control, audit trails, secure authentication and transparency around how documentation is generated. As AI becomes more widely used across software development, documentation is increasingly being linked directly to the development workflow rather than being treated as a separate task. title: WhatsApp Restricted Chat rolls out to Beta users on Android and iOS
content: Synopsis WhatsApp has started rolling out its new Restricted Chat feature to select beta users on Android and iOS, adding four restrictions designed to limit how messages and media can be accessed or handled within a conversation. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen ANI WhatsApp Restricted Chat rolls out to Beta users on Android and iOS WhatsApp has started rolling out its new Restricted Chat feature to select beta users on Android and iOS, adding four restrictions designed to limit how messages and media can be accessed or handled within a conversation. According to GSM Arena, Restricted Chat is available to some users running WhatsApp beta version 2.26.36.4 on Android and 26.39.10.20 on iOS. The feature was first reported last month as an upgrade to WhatsApp's Advanced Chat Privacy functionality. Restricted Chat is optional and does not apply to conversations by default. Users can manually enable it from the chat info screen for individual conversations. Once enabled, WhatsApp displays a message in the conversation and applies four restrictions. People in a Restricted Chat cannot automatically save media to their devices, export the chat, or use Meta AI features within the conversation. The feature also prevents participants from using linked devices for the chat. WhatsApp says, "this helps to prevent people in the chat from using unofficial clients or AI agents to access it," as cited by GSM Arena. WhatsApp has also clarified that enabling Restricted Chat does not change the encryption status of conversations. Messages and calls remain protected by end-to-end encryption , whether the feature is enabled or not. The Restricted Chat feature is currently limited to some users enrolled in WhatsApp's beta programme. WhatsApp has not yet indicated when it will be rolled out publicly to all users. title: AI deals seen driving medium-term growth as Indian IT sector faces muted Q2: Report
content: Synopsis India's IT services sector is likely to see muted performance in the second quarter of FY27, but increasing traction in artificial intelligence-related deals could support growth over the medium term, Centrum said in a report. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen ANI AI deals seen driving medium-term growth as Indian IT sector faces muted Q2: Report India's IT services sector is likely to see muted performance in the second quarter of FY27, but increasing traction in artificial intelligence-related deals could support growth over the medium term, Centrum said in a report. The report said the demand environment has remained broadly unchanged over the past three months, with clients cautious about AI adoption and longer decision-making timelines weighing on near-term growth. At the same time, the brokerage expects deal booking to remain healthy, with a strong pipeline across most IT services companies. "AI led deals to be significant drivers of incremental business growth in the medium term," the report said, pointing to the potential for the ongoing AI technology cycle to create new opportunities for Indian IT services companies. It expects the AI-led services market to reach USD 300-400 billion by 2030. However, the brokerage expects revenue growth across Tier 1 IT companies to remain subdued in the near term. title: BOJ says AI boom may have eased financial conditions, warns of market risks
content: Synopsis Bank of Japan Deputy Governor Shinichi Uchida said the global AI boom may have eased financial conditions by stoking demand and boosting asset prices, but warned of the risk of a market pullback if expected profits fail to materialize. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Reuters FILE PHOTO: Pedestrians walk past the Bank of Japan headquarters in Tokyo, Japan,September 18, 2026. Bank of Japan Deputy Governor Shinichi Uchida said the global AI boom may have eased financial conditions by stoking demand and boosting asset prices, but warned of the risk of a market pullback if expected profits fail to materialize. "It is a big positive demand shock, which has put upward pressure on the economy and prices," Uchida said on worldwide AI adoption in the text of a speech on the central bank's website on Monday. The technology could also raise productivity and enhance capital stock accumulation, which in turn might affect a country's natural rate of interest, he said. "Tentatively, it appears the demand side has come first and made financial conditions more accommodative on balance," Uchida said. "But there is a risk of correction if profits do not follow." While AI has boosted stock prices and made financial conditions easier, huge bond issuance by AI-related firms has put upward pressure on long-term interest rates, Uchida said. The BOJ will continue to carefully examine economic and financial data to ascertain a "consistent picture" on AI's impact, he said, adding that the overall effect on Japan's natural rate of interest was still hard to gauge. The BOJ has identified robust AI-related demand as among factors that could push underlying inflation above its 2% target, necessitating further monetary tightening. The central bank raised interest rates in June and September as the energy shock caused by the Iran war added to price pressures from a weak yen, which increases import costs. Japan imports almost all of its crude oil, of which most came from the Middle East before the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! title: White House AI task force will prevent 'overregulation': WSJ report
content: Synopsis A White House task force on artificial intelligence will assess the technology's risks and opportunities, while preventing overregulation that stifles innovation, its leader Jay Clayton has told the Wall Street Journal. The task force's charter states that it will "develop plans for responding to SI-enabled threats to our society, while preventing overregulation and regulatory capture that would stifle innovation and competition," according to the Journal. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen AP A White House task force on artificial intelligence will assess the technology's risks and opportunities, while preventing overregulation that stifles innovation, its leader Jay Clayton has told the Wall Street Journal. Clayton, the US director of national intelligence, is widely reported to be the new AI czar in the administration of US President Donald Trump, though the appointment is yet to be confirmed. Clayton would become the second person to hold the informal title after venture capitalist David Sacks, who held the role at the start of Trump's second term before stepping down. The new "Super Intelligence Force" -- using Trump's preferred term for artificial intelligence -- will have 120 days to report on the risks and opportunities of the technology, the Journal reported on Saturday. "The president asked that a group be put together that was going to ensure exactly what he said... (that) we stay the leaders in superintelligence, and that the interests of the American people are put first," Clayton said. "The risk of not being first is high," he added. "Not being first increases the identified, and unidentified, risks, particularly from our adversaries. Being first will better enable us to address those risks on behalf of the American people." A longtime Wall Street lawyer, Clayton represented Goldman Sachs during the 2008 financial crisis and Barclays in its purchase of Lehman Brothers' assets. Trump tapped Clayton to lead federal prosecutors in Manhattan at the start of his second term, and the Senate confirmed him as intelligence chief in July. He has no background in the tech industry. The task force's charter states that it will "develop plans for responding to SI-enabled threats to our society, while preventing overregulation and regulatory capture that would stifle innovation and competition," according to the Journal. It will also "recommend ways to improve the government's response capacity under existing authorities." Members of the task force include Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. title: Finnish town braces for change from Google data centres
content: Synopsis In the northern Finnish town of Muhos, 36-year-old farmer Joni Pitkanen is preparing for life with a new neighbour -- just kilometers away, tech giant Google is planning to build new data centres. The planned data centres are part of an announced 13-billion-euro ($15-billion) investment in Finland over the next two years -- the US tech giant's single biggest investment in Europe. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Agencies In the northern Finnish town of Muhos , 36-year-old farmer Joni Pitkanen is preparing for life with a new neighbour -- just kilometers away, tech giant Google is planning to build new data centres. The planned data centres are part of an announced 13-billion-euro ($15-billion) investment in Finland over the next two years -- the US tech giant's single biggest investment in Europe. A few kilometers down the gravel road that passes by Pitkanen's farm, the forest has already been cut down on land acquired by Google, with excavators now clearing the ground and rumbling trucks shuttling back and forth to the construction area located next to major power lines. "The project is so massive that it's basically hard to really grasp, even though we're right here on the sidelines," Pitkanen said, as a few cows dozed in a meadow in front of the barn. Google's expansion plans include the Finnish municipalities of Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala as well as Hamina, where it already operates a data centre. The massive investment prompted US President Donald Trump to urge Google to rethink its plans in a message on his Truth Social network. Pitkanen said he was so far "fairly positive" about the project, as it will bring "large-scale business activity" and "life" to the rural municipality with a population of only around 8,800 people. "But of course we are concerned about... how we can prepare for the energy consumption," he added. In his office in the small village centre, Muhos mayor Kimmo Hinno told AFP that Google's "massive investment" kept him busy these days as "no industry of this type" existed here at present. "This will completely change the situation for the entire municipality and the Oulu region," he said, adding that he expected "thousands of workers" of different nationalities during the construction period -- who will need both housing and other services. Outside a grocery store, 60-year-old nurse Aila Heilima said she hoped the investment would "motivate young people to stay" in Muhos for work, instead of moving to bigger towns in search of job opportunities. - Mounting criticism - But Google's plans have already sparked controversy. The Finnish Supervisory Agency (LVV) is currently investigating whether company Tuike Finland, which represents Google, had cleared more than 300 hectares of forest in Muhos without a mandatory environmental impact assessment. "In our view, operations at this construction site should be suspended until it is clarified whether the project is in compliance with the law," Hanna Halmeenpaa, chair of the board of the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation, who filed the request with the agency, told AFP at the edge of the deforested area. "From the satellite images, we've seen that nature sites which should be preserved have also been logged," she added, explaining that the size of the clear-cut area was comparable to 420 football fields. Google, meanwhile, told AFP in an email that "tree felling activities have been taking place in compliance with Forestry Act requirements" and they "were awaiting further guidance from LVV on this matter." "We have conducted extensive nature surveys covering the entire area as part of the zoning and Environmental Impact Assessment processes, to ensure high-value nature zones within the sites have been protected during forestry works," said Sondre Ronander, communications manager for Google in Finland. - Call for regulation - Finland has seen a spike in data centre investments, with its cool climate and relatively stable and cheap electricity that is mostly produced without fossil fuels thanks to nuclear plants as well as extensive wind and hydro power. Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's right-wing government has prioritised attracting data centre investments to the Nordic country, which is grappling with record-high unemployment and sluggish economic growth. But, as dozens of the energy guzzling centres are now under construction and many more planned by companies including Microsoft and TikTok, uncertainty around energy prices, grid capacity and environmental effects have sparked a public debate in Finland. A citizen's initiative demanding stricter regulation regarding data centre energy use and consequences for the environment gathered more than 50,000 signatures in just three days after it opened, meaning it will have to be reviewed by parliament. title: OpenAI's Sam Altman says AI benefits warrant accepting some risks
content: Synopsis OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman said the benefits of artificial intelligence justify accepting some risks and argued the technology should remain broadly accessible to the public " Listen to this article in summarized format Listen Agencies Sam Altman, CEO, OpenAI. OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman said the benefits of artificial intelligence justify accepting some risks and argued the technology should remain broadly accessible to the public. "We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency," Altman said in an interview with Politico's technology-focused newsletter Decoded. Altman said there remained a fundamental difference in worldview between OpenAI and rival Anthropic on AI regulation , adding: "I think there's a lot of daylight." "I disagree, but I understand the perspective of people who are like, 'This technology is going to get so powerful, and it's so dangerous, that a single lab in San Francisco should have it and make sure nothing bad happens, and kind of figure out how to dole out the benefits,'" Altman said. He called that "a completely unacceptable trade-off" that runs counter to the "lighter-touch regulatory stance" backed by OpenAI. "I wouldn't take a trade of saying, 'We'll make sure there's no major hacks, there's no misuse of this technology, there's zero scams, there's zero all the other bad things that will happen,'" Altman said. "Because I think people will do tremendously - orders of magnitude more - good stuff than bad stuff." Altman's remarks come amid a growing debate within the AI industry over the pace of development and the risks posed by increasingly capable systems. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei in September published an essay calling on the industry to slow down to "pace the frontier," a stance that Altman publicly endorsed. Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned in September, saying the people building AI believe it "could kill us all by the end of the decade. Reuters reported in September that Anthropic warned that, despite AI's potential benefits, the technology can sometimes act in ways that run counter to its makers' intentions and penetrate other companies' systems. The company said advanced models could exhibit "self-preserving behaviors," including attempts to "resist shutdown," "conceal or manipulate information," or generate outputs that could be interpreted as "coercive, deceptive, or manipulative." However, US President Donald Trump has largely dismissed calls for new restrictions, arguing they would make it harder for American companies to compete with Chinese rivals. He has repeatedly said existing law enforcement agencies, including the Justice Department, provide sufficient safeguards and that no new rules are needed. content: Synopsis In a letter to the boardâs chief executive officer, Indian Federation of App-based Transport Workers (IFAT) and Karnataka App-based Workers Union (KAWU) sought immediate rollout of health and accident insurance, income support during medical emergencies and temporary disablement, maternity benefits, scholarships for children of platform workers and an emergency distress fund. title: Spy chief Jay Clayton, the Trump loyalist tech bosses trust on AI
content: Synopsis The 60-year-old lawyer, who will keep his post as director of national intelligence, is unlikely to question the central place of artificial intelligence in the US economy, even as opposition to the technology grows among American voters. Listen to this article in summarized format Listen AP Jay Clayton , Donald Trump's pick for AI czar , is the nation's top spy, and a rare figure trusted by both the president and the tech bosses determined to keep the AI boom roaring. The 60-year-old lawyer, who will keep his post as director of national intelligence, is unlikely to question the central place of artificial intelligence in the US economy , even as opposition to the technology grows among American voters. "Jay Clayton is a golden asset for the administration because he's so well respected by tech leaders as well as many in the government," said Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co, an investment company. "He is not a typical Beltway bureaucrat," Ives added, calling the appointment "bullish for the industry because you can't just have a regular political appointee." A regular golf partner of Trump, Clayton entered politics when Trump picked him to lead the Securities and Exchange Commission, the national markets regulator, in 2017. A longtime Wall Street lawyer at Sullivan & Cromwell, where he represented Goldman Sachs during the 2008 financial crisis, Clayton ran the market regulator without ruffling feathers. He brought cases against crypto companies, an industry that has since become closely aligned with Trump and his family. His wife, Gretchen Butler Clayton, worked as a wealth manager at Goldman Sachs but stepped down when he joined the government in 2017. No David Sacks Trump picked Clayton to lead the US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York at the start of his second term, where he took on cases dear to the president, including a probe ordered by Trump into ties between prominent Democrats and the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. His office also signed off on controversial subpoenas against New York Times reporters days before his confirmation hearing for the intelligence post. The Senate confirmed him in July. But Clayton is no David Sacks, the Silicon Valley venture capitalist who held the AI role at the start of Trump's second term. Clayton has no technology background, but does hold an engineering degree from the University of Pennsylvania, where he also earned his law degree, as well as an economics degree from the University of Cambridge. "Jay Clayton doesn't have the same deep background in technology that Sacks brought to the role, but he has a rich federal resume and significant experience navigating the federal bureaucracy," said Aalok Mehta of the Center for Strategic and International Studies. "He also seems to be highly in sync with the president's thinking right now -- though of course we have seen plenty of examples of other advisors that started out that way but ultimately fell out of favor," Mehta added. Carl Tobias, a law professor at the University of Richmond, said juggling two major jobs would be a challenge, though Trump has handed multiple roles to trusted officials in his second term, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. National security "Jay Clayton ultimately is going to have to do what the president wants," said Connor Martin, a national security fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations. But by giving the AI portfolio to the nation's top spy, Trump seemed to be accepting arguments that the technology poses real dangers for cybersecurity and is key to the geopolitical rivalry with China, he added. A tech industry source in Washington said the industry largely welcomed the appointment, but cautioned against expecting major change. "Jay Clayton is not going to preside over some big regulatory effort," the source said. "If he brings coherence to the policy, or provides details that bring clarity, those would be wins." Clayton will not be the only voice in Trump's ear on AI, however. Sacks, along with tech bosses including Nvidia's Jensen Huang and Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, will continue to hold significant sway over how the president approaches the industry. Elon Musk is also back in Trump's good graces after their falling out in 2025. Clayton takes on the role days after tech bosses signed a commitment at the White House to self-police their AI models, an accord Trump called "morally binding." Mehta said he expected Clayton to coordinate the government more effectively while sticking to Trump's goal of not slowing the industry. "But at the same time, the problems he is facing -- like around AI safety and sentiment -- are bigger and harder now, and they are happening at a much faster clip," he said.
